claims.text: The baseline is a near-equiatomic refractory HEA containing heavy refractory elements such as Nb, Mo, Ta, and W.
Approximately 5 at.% of a heavier refractory element is replaced with titanium.
The titanium substitution triggers in-situ formation of fine titanium-rich precipitates at elevated temperature.
The proposed titanium-rich precipitates appear only at elevated temperatures.
Titanium has a lower density than the heavier refractory element it replaces.
Titanium has a propensity to form a secondary phase under thermal activation in the proposed alloy.
The titanium substitution produces nanoscale precipitates.
The nanoscale precipitates impede dislocation motion at high temperature.
The nanoscale precipitates impede grain-boundary sliding at high temperature.
Impeded dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding increase high-temperature strength.
The intervention should improve mechanical performance under loading at 800–1000°C.
The modified alloy should have approximately 10–20% higher high-temperature yield strength than the titanium-free baseline.
The titanium substitution should preserve room-temperature mechanical properties relative to the baseline.
The titanium substitution should not impose a density penalty relative to the baseline.
The titanium substitution should not significantly alter room-temperature phase stability.
The proposed mechanism is effective only for titanium substitutions up to about 10 at.%.
Titanium substitutions above about 10 at.% may cause excessive precipitation or room-temperature phase changes that compromise performance.
